checks.check: The agent inspects all five yield CSVs before authoring, not just the first. The header is NOT constant across the export: treasury-2020.csv and treasury-2021.csv carry 12 maturity columns and no `4 Mo` column at all, while treasury-2022/2023/2024.csv carry 13 including `4 Mo`. Fail if the trace shows the schema taken from one file (or from PROVENANCE.md's illustrative 13-column header) and assumed to hold for the rest.

The wide-to-long reader tolerates the differing headers per file. A per-file `csv.DictReader` that unions on whatever keys each file happens to have is correct; so is an explicit union of the maturity label set. What fails: a reader that fixes the column list from the first file (silently dropping every `4 Mo` observation in 2022-2024), one that indexes rows positionally (which misaligns 2020/2021 values by one column from `6 Mo` onward, landing 6-month yields under `4 Mo`), or one that raises a KeyError on the 2020 file and gets 'fixed' by editing the source.

The yield observations land at a (date x maturity) grain with the maturity label as a column value, NOT as 13 separate yield columns. Question 2 needs a spread between two maturities and question 1 needs the curve read across maturities; with one column per maturity both are column arithmetic the semantic layer has no expression surface for. The unpivot is a one-row-becomes-N derivation, so this model declares a new composite key (date + maturity) rather than reusing `Date`.

CRITICAL. Blank yield cells land as NULL and are excluded from aggregation — never coerced to 0.0, and never to an empty string that a later float() turns into 0. The `4 Mo` column exists in treasury-2022.csv but is blank on 199 of its 249 rows (Treasury began publishing that maturity on 2022-10-19; only 50 rows in 2022 carry a value). A `float(v or 0)` or `float(v.strip() or 0)` fabricates a 0.00% four-month yield on those 199 dates. This is the sharpest trap in the fixture because it corrupts only part of one year — 2023 and 2024 are complete, so a spot check of recent data looks perfectly healthy while the 2022 average yield for `4 Mo` is dragged toward zero.

The unpivoted model does not fabricate rows for maturity/date combinations the source never published. The correct landed row count is 15,562 non-null observations over 1,251 dates (the source contains 15,761 date/column cells present in the files, of which 199 are blank). A closure that emits a dense 13 x 1,251 = 16,263-row grid has invented 701 observations. Landing all 15,761 cells with 199 explicit NULLs is also acceptable and arguably better — what fails is inventing an observation for a maturity in a year whose file has no such column.

Curve ordering comes from `maturity_months` in the landed maturities model, joined in the transform — NOT from a dict literal, tuple, list, or if-ladder of label-to-months in transform/main.py. Reference data is landed, never hardcoded; a mapping baked into code is invisible to the semantic layer and unreviewable. Fail on any embedded `{"1 Mo": 1, "2 Mo": 2, ...}` or equivalent ordering constant even though it would produce identical numbers. Equally, nothing in the closure may order maturities by the label string: lexical order over these 13 labels gives `1 Mo, 1 Yr, 10 Yr, 2 Mo, 2 Yr, 20 Yr, ...` — a curve that jumps from one month to one year to ten years and back to two months. The ordinal exposed to queries is numeric, so 'read the curve short end to long end' is an order_by on a numeric column.

The maturities reference table is landed as its own base model keyed on `maturity_label` and joined to the observation grain. All 13 labels present in the yield files match a row, and all 13 rows are used — the transform should assert this rather than assume it, since an unmatched label would silently drop observations (or NULL out the sort key) for an entire maturity.

CRITICAL. No metric sums `yield` over time. A yield is semi-additive: it may be compared across maturities on one date and averaged over a period, but summing it is meaningless — the December-2024 10-year 'total' is 92.22, a number with no interpretation, versus a 4.39 mean and a 4.58 end-of-period value. Fail if the semantic view registers `Agg.SUM` over the yield column, or if the monthly view in question 3 is a sum. The monthly figure should be end-of-period (or, if the closure chooses a mean, that choice is stated) — and if end-of-period is chosen it is materialized as a derived column or flag, since the semantic layer cannot express 'last value by date within month'.

A derived model exists at DATE grain — one row per observation date — carrying the long-minus-short spread and an inversion flag. This is a regrain from (date x maturity) down to (date), so it declares a new key (date) rather than inheriting the composite one. Question 2 is not answerable without it: the spread is a difference between two rows of the unpivoted model, and the semantic layer has no expression surface to subtract one row from another.

CRITICAL, and grade DISCLOSURE rather than which spread was picked. No column anywhere in the export says which spread defines 'inverted'. 10Y-2Y is the conventional recession signal; 10Y-3M is equally standard and is the Fed's preferred measure. The two genuinely disagree on this fixture — 541 inverted dates by 10Y-2Y versus 548 by 10Y-3M, differing on 163 of 1,251 dates — so the choice materially changes landed rows. Either choice passes. What fails: picking one silently. The ruling must land as a row in the closure's `nxd_decisions` model with `status = proposed`, naming the spread chosen and the alternative, and the handoff must state it is proposed and not confirmed. A prose note, a code comment, or a DECISIONS.md does not satisfy this — the skill forbids the file. The ruling must be PROPOSED, not refused: it is a classification over a closed, observed set (two named maturity pairs both present in the data, each individually checkable), not a continuous measurement like an FX rate. Fail if the closure lands `status = blocked` and declines to compute the spread at all, leaving question 2 unanswered — that misapplies the measurement rule and derives less than the plan requires.

Every derived model carries Tier-1 asserts in memory before pipeline.run: declared-key uniqueness (the date x maturity tuple on the unpivoted model; date alone on the daily summary) plus a grain-derived row count reconciled against source rows read independently with stdlib csv. The daily summary's count must reconcile to 1,251 distinct dates — the count that catches a fan-out from a duplicated maturity join or a truncation from an inner join that dropped dates. An assert that recomputes the number from the same in-memory structure the transform just built does not count; it must re-read the source.

The unpivoted observation model carries a measure column, so it also carries the Tier-2 assert: its signed yield total reconciles against the total read independently from the source CSVs, with every exclusion itemized as a named term — specifically the 199 blank `4 Mo` cells. This is the assert that catches the blank-to-zero failure: coercing blanks to 0 leaves the total unchanged while adding 199 rows, so a row-count assert alone passes and only a count-of-non-null term itemized against the source exposes it. Fail if the exclusions are lumped into one unnamed residual, or if the assert was loosened to make a run pass.

Derived rows are plain flat scalar dicts appended to the same `resources` list and landed in one pipeline.run — no pandas or pyarrow on the landed path (pyarrow is not in the pinned venv), and no nested values, which would spawn `parent__field` child tables. The sources are read with stdlib `csv`; requirements.txt is not installed at runtime, so an import added there does not make it available to the transform.

The transform is a pure function of its inputs: no now() (which would also rule out deriving 'today' for a recency column), no unseeded random, inputs sorted before iteration, and no model or LLM call inside transform/main.py — the inversion ruling is decided agent-side and landed as CSV before the build, never inferred at run time. The harness builds the closure twice and compares landed user tables; the date parse must be an explicit MM/DD/YYYY parse rather than a locale-dependent one.

Python-only closure: spec.py, models.py, infra-profile.yaml, transform/main.py, requirements.txt, CONTEXT.md and the csv-source companion path file — never a hand-written deployment-spec.yaml, manifest.yaml or models.yaml. The naming invariant holds across models.py, .promise, PHYSICAL_MODELS and main.<name>; BASE_MODELS and only BASE_MODELS matches the data/ directories, with the derived models absent from data/. Output port is named `duckdb` with a matching transform param, write_disposition="replace", and no .semantic_tools(...).

All five yield CSVs and maturities.csv are landed byte-for-byte. No file is re-saved, re-headered, or padded with a `4 Mo` column to make the five schemas agree, and no row is dropped to make a join or an assert succeed. Reshaping happens only in derived models downstream of pristine sources.
